Thanks to the authors for the detailed responses. However, my concerns are still not well addressed.

In other words, my main concern in the original review is about **the value and applicability of this study**. I understand the authors’ claims that *“the scope of our study is to show that models already possess the ability to exploit such input patterns even during inference”* and that *“our paper aims to understand how a model’s performance changes when filler tokens are inserted into the input, and at no point was the model trained on filler tokens.”* However, the current experimental results of this study do not yet seem applicable or insightful to the community. The reasons are twofold:
1. Directly inserting filler tokens at inference time leads to inconsistent performance fluctuations, which cannot provide clear guidance for subsequent researchers or users seeking performance gains. Given the fluctuating performance after inserting filler tokens, I also wonder whether similar fluctuations would occur if we instead inserted some noise text (e.g., “aaaaa” or meaningful but irrelevant text) at inference time.
2. If the authors could demonstrate that current LLMs can be significantly enhanced by lightweight fine-tuning on filler tokens, I would consider this study more applicable and beneficial. However, the experiments in Figure 4 and Figure 5 show that the required training is highly computationally demanding while the performance gains are marginal, which makes me believe that the value of this study still needs further improvement.

Therefore, I prefer to keep my original score.

Thank you for your reply and for clarifying the questions we raised. Based on your response, I think I can tentatively understand your paper as aiming to reveal certain phenomena, rather than to propose an algorithm that can be directly used in practice at this moment. If the phenomena are sufficiently “solid” and one can reasonably foresee their potential future value, then I would consider this an excellent piece of research (even if there is currently no new algorithm).

However, the problem now is that I cannot imagine what kind of potential value such a finding would ultimately bring. It seems that any algorithms it might give rise to in the future could all be replaced by CoT, or would run into token capacity limitations (as you mentioned in the paper, where performance drops significantly after adding 256 padding tokens).

As for the differences between PT/IT that you describe in the paper, I believe they merely reflect, from another angle, a common consensus in the field, namely that in the IT stage the model acquires instruction-following and reasoning abilities far beyond those obtained in the PT stage.

Moreover, and most importantly, I believe that attributing “inconsistency of effects” to “model family/type” is a fundamental mistake. It is like asking a large model a question: different types of models will give different answers, and models from the same family (because they share part of the training data) will give similar answers. This is something we would naturally expect. In other words, I could also study various variants such as “repeating each decoded token n times during inference,” “inserting random symbols after each generated token during inference,” or “inserting random symbols after each token in the prefill stage,” and so on. But if no consistent conclusion is obtained, then all such work can only be regarded as experimental reports, and at the very least are not suitable for publication at a top conference like ICLR.

We once again thank the reviewers for replying to each reviewer’s comments in such detail, but at the same time I also hope the authors will seriously reflect on why all four reviewers gave consistent evaluations of the initial submission. Please acknowledge the parts of the paper that were not done sufficiently well. Since it is possible to upload a new manuscript during the rebuttal period, please mark the new changes you make in colored text.

If you feel that any of the above points diverge from your understanding of my opinion, I would be very happy to discuss them with you further.

summary.value: This paper investigates whether LLMs can leverage manually inserted filler tokens (such as <pad>, \t, \n ...) at inference time to enhance their reasoning performance. The authors conduct experiments on 6 types of filler tokens on varying sizes of LLMs, revealing even filler tokens can lead to performance variations, especially for small size LLMs.

strengths.value:
1. The writing and structure of this paper are clear and easy to understand.
2. The research question is interesting. It would be attractive if we find that this approach can consistently boost the performance of LLMs through simple prompt manipulation.

weaknesses.value:
1. The main weakness of this paper is that the performance of LLMs after injecting filler tokens varies. Some LLMs perform better on MMLU and ARC after injecting filler tokens, while others do not. The authors neither explain nor analyze this phenomenon (Section 4.4 reads more like a case study than a rigorous analysis), nor do they make efforts to avoid performance degradation in a training-free manner. As a result, the proposed approach appears to add random manipulation to the input prompt rather than serving as a convincing, beneficial algorithm that can consistently enhance LLM performance.
2. Although the authors show that the performance of OLMo-2 can be enhanced by filler-token fine-tuning in Section 4.3, it requires large-scale pretraining and instruction tuning, while the performance gain is marginal (~1% in Figure 5) compared to the heavy computational cost. This also somewhat deviates from the main goal of the paper, which is enhancing LLM performance by expanding computation space at inference time. Furthermore, this validation is only conducted on one LLM with one filler token, making it unclear whether the training can generalize.
3. Typo: in Line 218, GSM8K contains 1319 test set examples, not 1819.

> 1) my main concern for this work is that the contribution seems weak - the number of tokens, and the type of tokens do not seem to show general patterns that adds meaningful findings to the community. Would the authors can clarify them better in case I missed something or undermined the points?

Our study does not propose a method for improving reasoning. Rather, it investigates whether LLMs possess the ability to make use of seemingly meaningless filler tokens—even when such inputs were never encountered during PT or IT.

Although this input format was never seen during training, we investigated how an expanded input space affects model performance. This was something that prior work could not reveal, and we examined whether models improve when given such expanded input space, as well as which token types influence performance for different model sizes. Our findings show that, despite appearing useless, the expanded space actually directs attention to important parts of the input—as seen in the attention maps—and this phenomenon indeed contributes to performance improvements.

By evaluating checkpoints from the very beginning to the end of PT and IT, we confirmed that the performance of this input format is fundamentally influenced by the model’s inherent capability, but becomes beneficial once the model has acquired a certain level of linguistic proficiency (after PT). These results suggest that, similar to prior work, if models were trained on this type of input format, they could achieve even stronger performance.

summary.value: This paper investigates the impact of adding filler tokens across types, counts, and positions. It also examines when during training this phenomenon emerges. Attention-map analysis shows that these tokens focus on relevant parts of the input and help the model arrive at the answer.

strengths.value:
- The paper examines the impact of expanding computation space by adding filler tokens at inference time.

- It reports observations across several factors, including model type and size, as well as token types and counts.

weaknesses.value:
The overall patterns of results and explanations are not consistent across model types and sizes, as well as token types and counts.

- The explanations are sometimes inconsistent. For example, for Qwen2.5-14B vs. 32B, the paper argues that larger models benefit from filler tokens, yet for SmolLM (1.7B) it claims the additional tokens are “effectively utilized for reasoning,” suggesting a different rationale for small models. In line with this concern, more experiments are needed to substantiate the claims. 

- The paper argues that additional tokens compensate for limited parameters in small models, but it evaluates only SmolLM as the “small model.” More small models should be tested to support generalization. 

- Several reported patterns do not generalize well. For instance, the paper claims that adding more than 64 <pad> tokens degrades performance, attributing this to its rarity during training. However, repetition of other tokens may also be rare in typical training data. 

- According to Llama’s explanation of <pad> vs. <eos>, the training dataset influences these patterns. However, the impact of filler tokens in Qwen2.5-14B and 32B does not align, even though they are from the same model family.

- The checkpoint analysis shows no clear trends. Pretraining (PT) checkpoints do not improve with filler tokens, while instruction-tuning (IT) checkpoints likewise fail to show a consistent pattern of improvement across the training process. 

- The attention map analysis hardly explains why the improvements occurred. Strong attention alone does not necessarily translate into better performance. Even so, the paper should present counterexamples (e.g., cases where the model answers incorrectly) and, where possible, quantify these patterns.

summary.value: This paper investigates whether large language models can leverage artificially inserted filler tokens—without any additional training—to enhance reasoning performance. Building on the intuition that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting benefits not only from explicit reasoning steps but also from the larger “computational space” of longer inputs, the authors systematically study what kinds, amounts, and insertion locations of filler tokens are effective. Through experiments across multiple open-domain QA and math benchmarks using models from 1.7B to 32B parameters, they find that inserting familiar filler characters (e.g., spaces, newlines, dashes) directly before the final Answer: token can significantly improve accuracy, especially in smaller models (up to +12.37 percentage points). Attention-map analyses reveal that these expanded spaces participate in meaningful computation, continuing or redirecting attention toward relevant parts of the problem.

strengths.value:
1. The experiments cover two categories of tasks—QA (MMLU, ARC) and mathematics (GSM8K, MATH-500)—using a range of instruction-tuned models from small to large (including Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct). Results are reported in a zero-shot setting averaged over three random seeds. For multiple-choice questions, the answer is extracted by applying a softmax over the final-layer logits of options A–D, and for math problems, the numerical answer is extracted following existing evaluation rules. The evaluation interface is fully transparent.

2. A comprehensive factor analysis is conducted: systematic ablations are performed on token type (space, newline, tab, period, <pad>, dash), quantity, and insertion position, revealing several consistent experimental patterns.

3. A preliminary set of actionable guidelines is provided, summarizing multiple practical insights with direct reference value for deployment.

weaknesses.value:
1. I am confused and skeptical about the motivation of the paper. If the goal is to alleviate the time consumption caused by the lack of parallelism in CoT reasoning, then according to the experimental results reported in the paper, this method seems to save only about the generation time of 256 tokens, which appears to bring minimal benefit for long-text reasoning. If the goal is to propose an alternative to CoT, the paper lacks direct comparative experiments on the answer quality obtained by CoT.

2. The authors should add a “same token budget” comparison with CoT: the paper does not take CoT prompts with the same number of tokens as a baseline for direct comparison, making it difficult to answer the key question of whether ECS performs better (or worse) than short CoT under the same token or time cost. The current results mostly verify that “merely adding positions can bring gains,” but if ECS does not show clear advantages over CoT in some aspects, its practical value will be greatly discounted.

3. The paper has not yet summarized general, actionable insights that are independent of specific tasks.

questions.value: Could the decline in accuracy with an increasing number of tokens in the ECS be related to the inherent difficulty of the problem itself? Perhaps the additional tokens cause the model to overthink, leading it to second-guess its own reasoning.

Our input (solid line) shows a performance trend similar to the no–filler-token condition (dashed line). This indicates that our methodology depends on the model’s inherent capabilities. What is noteworthy is that, during the PT phase, the performance generally aligns with the model’s baseline but fluctuates, whereas in the IT phase, although the trend is similar, it consistently outperforms the baseline. How inserted tokens expand the model’s computational space can be observed through the attention map examples. In Figure 6, the lower triangular region corresponds to the inserted tokens, and we can see cases where high attention scores are directed toward important parts of the actual input. Moreover, different attention heads assign attention to different aspects: tokens representing answer candidates such as A, B, C, and D; the parts of the input that provide crucial hints; and functional elements of the input such as eot. This shows that inserted tokens are not meaningless—rather, they help the model make important decisions within the input.

Similarly, in Figure 9, even when as many as 64 tokens are inserted (the lower triangular region), we can still observe that the model attends to the key parts of the input (bright sky-blue, white, and pale-colored regions).

We were also cautious about the possibility that even small prompt variations could change a model's output. Therefore, to verify that the effects of filler tokens were consistent, we conducted experiments with three different seeds. This is because our study aims to extend the input artificially during inference without the model having learned such patterns. Based on previous studies showing that a model trained on a certain amount of completely random tokens can achieve performance comparable to CoT, we can infer that performance drops occur because the model is unfamiliar with this type of dataset. Interestingly, however, we found that some models possess a latent ability to utilize these tokens even without prior training, and that increasing the input space for smaller models can enhance their performance. Additionally, the performance drop observed with longer inputs does not only apply to the additional tokens but also seems to stem from the “lost-in-the-middle” problem common in transformer-based models.

If the goal is to alleviate the time consumption caused by the lack of parallelism in CoT reasoning, then according to the experimental results reported in the paper, this method seems to save only about the generation time of 256 tokens, which appears to bring minimal benefit for long-text reasoning. If the goal is to propose an alternative to CoT, the paper lacks direct comparative experiments on the answer quality obtained by CoT.

> The authors should add a “same token budget” comparison with CoT: the paper does not take CoT prompts with the same number of tokens as a baseline for direct comparison, making it difficult to answer the key question of whether ECS performs better (or worse) than short CoT under the same token or time cost. The current results mostly verify that “merely adding positions can bring gains,” but if ECS does not show clear advantages over CoT in some aspects, its practical value will be greatly discounted.

The study of replacing filler tokens with CoT prompts has already been conducted in [1]. However, in that study, the model had never been trained on specifically transformed filler tokens, so they created additional synthetic datasets for training and reported performance comparable to CoT on certain tasks. Inspired by this, we started our research with the idea that additional input space itself might be utilized by the model for reasoning.

However, without such training, adding a reasoning trajectory (CoT) input to the model naturally contains more information than seemingly meaningless filler tokens, so it inevitably yields better performance; thus, we did not treat them as directly comparable. In fact, the results in Figure 3 include CoT prompt inputs provided by the datasets for both Math500 and GSM8K. When CoT inputs were entirely removed, the EM scores dropped below roughly 10%, highlighting the large performance gap between having CoT and not having it. Nevertheless, whether CoT was included or not, we observed performance improvements when filler tokens were additionally provided. This shows that while it is unreasonable to replace CoT entirely with filler tokens if the model has not learned the filler token format, filler tokens can still contribute to performance improvements when used in addition to CoT.
